of the truly great mind about you, Tuppence. Fire ahead. I’m listening.”"}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "“To begin with,” said Tuppence, “what have we to go upon?”"}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“Absolutely nothing,” said Tommy cheerily."}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "“Wrong!” Tuppence wagged an energetic finger. “We have two distinct
clues.”"}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "“What are they?”"}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "“First clue, we know one of the gang.”"}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "“Whittington?”"}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "“Yes. don’t know where to look for him, and it’s about a thousand to one

noticed that once coincidences start happening they go on happening in
the most extraordinary way. I dare say it’s some natural law that we
haven’t found out. Still, as you say, we can’t rely on that. But there
_are_ places in London where simply every one is bound to turn up sooner
or later. Piccadilly Circus, for instance. One of my ideas was to take
up my stand there every day with a tray of flags.”"}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "“What about meals?” inquired the practical Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“How like a man! one’s got a better appetite than you have, Tuppence, and by tea-time
you’d be eating the flags, pins and all. But, honestly, I don’t think
much of the idea. Whittington mayn’t be in London at all.”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“That’s true. Anyway, I think clue No. 2 is more promising.”"}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“Let’s hear it.”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“It’s nothing much. Only a Christian name--Rita. Whittington mentioned
it that day.”"}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“Are you proposing a third advertisement: Wanted, female crook,
answering to the name of Rita?”"}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "“I am not. I propose to reason in a logical manner. That man, Danvers,
was shadowed on the way over, wasn’t he? And it’s more likely to have
been a woman than a man----”"}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“I don’t see that at all.”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“I am absolutely certain that it would be a woman, and a good-looking
one,” replied Tuppence calmly."}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "“On these technical points I bow to your decision,” murmured Mr.

it to Mr. Carter. I got his reply this morning, and among other things
it encloses the official statement of those saved from the _Lusitania_.
How’s that for clever little Tuppence?”"}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“Full marks for industry, zero for modesty. But the great point is, is

Christian names are given. mounted the ramshackle staircase. Everything in the house was filthy

hung in loose festoons from the wall. In every angle was a grey mass of
cobweb."}, {"paragraph": 2, "text": "Tommy proceeded leisurely. By the time he reached the bend of the
staircase, he had heard the man below disappear into a back room.
Clearly no suspicion attached to him as yet. To come to the house and
ask for “Mr. Brown” appeared indeed to be a reasonable and natural
proceeding."}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": "At the top of the stairs Tommy halted to consider his next move. In
front of him ran a narrow passage, with doors opening on either side of
it. From the one nearest him on the left came a low murmur of voices.
It was this room which he had been directed to enter. But what held
his glance fascinated was a small recess immediately on his right,
half concealed by a torn velvet curtain. It was directly opposite the
left-handed door and, owing to its angle, it also commanded a good view
of the upper part of the staircase. As a hiding-place for one or, at a
pinch, two men, it was ideal, being about two feet deep and three feet
wide. It attracted Tommy mightily. He thought things over in his usual
slow and steady way, deciding that the mention of “Mr. Brown” was not a
request for an individual, but in all probability a password used by
the gang. His lucky use of it had gained him admission. So far he had
aroused no suspicion. But he must decide quickly on his next step."}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "Suppose he were boldly to enter the room on the left of the passage.
Would the mere fact of his having been admitted to the house be
sufficient? Perhaps a further password would be required, or, at any
rate, some proof of identity. The doorkeeper clearly did not know all
the members of the gang by sight, but it might be different upstairs.
On the whole it seemed to him that luck had served him very well so far,
but that there was such a thing as trusting it too far. To enter
that room was a colossal risk. He could not hope to sustain his part
indefinitely; sooner or later he was almost bound to betray himself, and
then he would have thrown away a vital chance in mere foolhardiness."}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "A repetition of the signal knock sounded on the door below, and Tommy,
his mind made up, slipped quickly into the recess, and cautiously drew
the curtain farther across so that it shielded him completely from
sight. There were several rents and slits in the ancient material which
afforded him a good view. He would watch events, and any time he chose
could, after all, join the assembly, modelling his behaviour on that of
the new arrival."}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "The man who came up the staircase with a furtive, soft-footed tread was
quite unknown to Tommy. He was obviously of the very dregs of society.
The low beetling brows, and the criminal jaw, the bestiality of the
whole countenance were new to the young man, though he was a type that
Scotland Yard would have recognized at a glance."}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "The man passed the recess, breathing heavily as he went. He stopped at
the door opposite, and gave a repetition of the signal knock. A voice
inside called out something, and the man opened the door and passed in,
affording Tommy a momentary glimpse of the room inside. He thought there
must be about four or five people seated round a long table that took up
most of the space, but his attention was caught and held by a tall man
with close-cropped hair and a short, pointed, naval-looking beard,
who sat at the head of the table with papers in front of him. As the
new-comer entered he glanced up, and with a correct, but curiously
precise enunciation, which attracted Tommy’s notice, he asked:"}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "“Your number, comrade?”"}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“Fourteen, gov’nor,” replied the other hoarsely."}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "“Correct.”"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "The door shut again."}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "“If that isn’t a Hun, I’m a Dutchman!” said Tommy to himself. “And
running the show darned systematically too--as they always do. Lucky I
didn’t roll in. I’d have given the wrong number, and there would have
been the deuce to pay. No, this is the place for me. Hullo, here’s
another knock.”"}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "This visitor proved to be of an entirely different type to the last.
Tommy recognized in him an Irish Sinn Feiner. Certainly Mr. Brown’s
organization was a far-reaching concern. The common criminal, the
well-bred Irish gentleman, the pale Russian, and the efficient German
master of the ceremonies! Truly a strange and sinister gathering! Who
was this man who held in his finger these curiously variegated links of
an unknown chain?"}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "In this case, the procedure was exactly the same. The signal knock, the
demand for a number, and the reply “Correct.”"}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "Two knocks followed in quick succession on the door below. The first man
was quite unknown to Tommy, who put him down as a city clerk. A quiet,
intelligent-looking man, rather shabbily dressed. The second was of the
working classes, and his face was vaguely familiar to the young man."}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "Three minutes later came another, a man of commanding appearance,
exquisitely dressed, and evidently well born. His face, again, was not
unknown to the watcher, though he could not for the moment put a name to
it."}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "After his arrival there was a long wait. In fact Tommy concluded that
the gathering was now complete, and was just cautiously creeping out
from his hiding-place, when another knock sent him scuttling back to
cover."}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "This last-comer came up the stairs so quietly that he was almost abreast
of Tommy before the young man had realized his presence."}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "He was a small man, very pale, with a gentle almost womanish air. The
angle of the cheek-bones hinted at his Slavonic ancestry, otherwise
there was nothing to indicate his nationality. As he passed the recess,
he turned his head slowly. The strange light eyes seemed to burn through
the curtain; Tommy could hardly believe that the man did not know he was
there and in spite of himself he shivered. He was no more fanciful than
the majority of young Englishmen, but he could not rid himself of the
impression that some unusually potent force emanated from the man. The
creature reminded him of a venomous snake."}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "A moment later his impression was proved correct. The new-comer knocked
on the door as all had done, but his reception was very different. The
bearded man rose to his feet, and all the others followed suit. The
German came forward and shook hands. His heels clicked together."}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "“We are honoured,” he said. “We are greatly honoured. I much feared that
it would be impossible.”"}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "The other answered in a low voice that had a kind of hiss in it:"}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“There were difficulties. It will not be possible again, I fear. But one
meeting is essential--to define my policy. I can do nothing without--Mr.
Brown. He is here?”"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "The change in the German’s voice was audible as he replied with slight
hesitation:"}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "“We have received a message. It is impossible for him to be present
in person.” He stopped, giving a curious impression of having left the
sentence unfinished."}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "A very slow smile overspread the face of the other. He looked round at a
circle of uneasy faces."}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "“Ah! I understand. I have read of his methods. He works in the dark and
trusts no one. But, all the same, it is possible that he is among us
now....” He looked round him again, and again that expression of fear
swept over the group. Each man seemed eyeing his neighbour doubtfully."}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "The Russian tapped his cheek."}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "“So be it. Let us proceed.”"}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "The German seemed to pull himself together. He indicated the place he
had been occupying at the head of the table. The Russian demurred, but
the other insisted."}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "“It is the only possible place,” he said, “for--Number One. Perhaps
Number Fourteen will shut the door?”"}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "In another moment Tommy was once more confronting bare wooden panels,
and the voices within had sunk once more to a mere undistinguishable
murmur. Tommy became restive. The conversation he had overheard had
stimulated his curiosity. He felt that, by hook or by crook, he must
hear more."}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "There was no sound from below, and it did not seem likely that the
doorkeeper would come upstairs. After listening intently for a minute or
two, he put his head round the curtain. The passage was deserted. Tommy
bent down and removed his shoes, then, leaving them behind the curtain,
he walked gingerly out on his stockinged feet, and kneeling down by
the closed door he laid his ear cautiously to the crack. To his intense
annoyance he could distinguish little more; just a chance word here and
there if a voice was raised, which merely served to whet his curiosity
still farther."}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "He eyed the handle of the door tentatively. Could he turn it by degrees
so gently and imperceptibly that those in the room would notice nothing?
He decided that with great care it could be done. Very slowly, a
fraction of an inch at a time, he moved it round, holding his breath in
his excessive care. A little more--a little more still--would it never
be finished? Ah! at last it would turn no farther."}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "He stayed so for a minute or two, then drew a deep breath, and pressed
it ever so slightly inward. The door did not budge. Tommy was annoyed.
If he had to use too much force, it would almost certainly creak.
He waited until the voices rose a little, then he tried again. Still
nothing happened. He increased the pressure. Had the beastly thing
stuck? Finally, in desperation, he pushed with all his might. But the
door remained firm, and at last the truth dawned upon him. It was locked
or bolted on the inside."}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "For a moment or two Tommy’s indignation got the better of him."}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“Well, I’m damned!” he said. “What a dirty trick!”"}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "As his indignation cooled, he prepared to face the situation. Clearly
the first thing to be done was to restore the handle to its original
position. If he let it go suddenly, the men inside would be almost
certain to notice it, so, with the same infinite pains, he reversed his
former tactics. All went well, and with a sigh of relief the young man
rose to his feet. There was a certain bulldog tenacity about Tommy that
made him slow to admit defeat. Checkmated for the moment, he was far
from abandoning the conflict. He still intended to hear what was going
on in the locked room. As one plan had failed, he must hunt about for
another."}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "He looked round him. A little farther along the passage on the left was
a second door. He slipped silently along to it. He listened for a moment
or two, then tried the handle. It yielded, and he slipped inside."}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "The room, which was untenanted, was furnished as a bedroom. Like
everything else in the house, the furniture was falling to pieces, and
the dirt was, if anything, more abundant."}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "But what interested Tommy was the thing he had hoped to find, a
communicating door between the two rooms, up on the left by the window.
Carefully closing the door into the passage behind him, he stepped
across to the other and examined it closely. The bolt was shot across
it. It was very rusty, and had clearly not been used for some time. By
gently wriggling it to and fro, Tommy managed to draw it back without
making too much noise. Then he repeated his former manœuvres with the
handle--this time with complete success. The door swung open--a crack,
a mere fraction, but enough for Tommy to hear what went on. There was a
velvet _portière_ on the inside of this door which prevented him from
seeing, but he was able to recognize the voices with a reasonable amount
of accuracy."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "The Sinn Feiner was speaking. His rich Irish voice was unmistakable:"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“That’s all very well. But more money is essential. No money--no
results!”"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "Another voice which Tommy rather thought was that of Boris replied:"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“Will you guarantee that there _are_ results?”"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“In a month from now--sooner or later as you wish--I will guarantee you
such a reign of terror in Ireland as shall shake the British Empire to
its foundations.”"}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "There was a pause, and then came the soft, sibilant accents of Number
One:"}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“Good! You shall have the money. Boris, you will see to that.”"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "Boris asked a question:"}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "“Via the Irish Americans, and Mr. Potter as usual?”"}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“I guess that’ll be all right!” said a new voice, with a transatlantic
intonation, “though I’d like to point out, here and now, that things
are getting a mite difficult. There’s not the sympathy there was, and
a growing disposition to let the Irish settle their own affairs without
interference from America.”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "Tommy felt that Boris had shrugged his shoulders as he answered:"}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“Does that matter, since the money only nominally comes from the
States?”"}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "“The chief difficulty is the landing of the ammunition,” said the Sinn
Feiner. “The money is conveyed in easily enough--thanks to our colleague
here.”"}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "Another voice, which Tommy fancied was that of the tall,
commanding-looking man whose face had seemed familiar to him, said:"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "“Think of the feelings of Belfast if they could hear you!”"}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“That is settled, then,” said the sibilant tones. “Now, in the matter
of the loan to an English newspaper, you have arranged the details
satisfactorily, Boris?”"}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "“I think so.”"}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“That is good. An official denial from Moscow will be forthcoming if
necessary.”"}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "There was a pause, and then the clear voice of the German broke the
silence:"}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "“I am directed by--Mr. Brown, to place the summaries of the reports
from the different unions before you. That of the miners is most
satisfactory. We must hold back the railways. There may be trouble with
the A.S.E.”"}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "For a long time there was a silence, broken only by the rustle of papers
and an occasional word of explanation from the German. Then Tommy heard
the light tap-tap of fingers, drumming on the table."}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "“And--the date, my friend?” said Number One."}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": "“The 29th.”"}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": "The Russian seemed to consider:"}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "“That is rather soon.”"}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“I know. But it was settled by the principal Labour leaders, and we
cannot seem to interfere too much. They must believe it to be entirely
their own show.”"}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "The Russian laughed softly, as though amused."}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“Yes, yes,” he said. “That is true. They must have no inkling that we
are using them for our own ends. They are honest men--and that is their
value to us. It is curious--but you cannot make a revolution without
honest men. The instinct of the populace is infallible.” He paused, and
then repeated, as though the phrase pleased him: “Every revolution has
had its honest men. They are soon disposed of afterwards.”"}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "There was a sinister note in his voice."}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "The German resumed:"}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“Clymes must go. He is too far-seeing. Number Fourteen will see to
that.”"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "There was a hoarse murmur."}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“That’s all right, gov’nor.” And then after a moment or two: “Suppose
I’m nabbed.”"}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“You will have the best legal talent to defend you,” replied the
German quietly. “But in any case you will wear gloves fitted with the
finger-prints of a notorious housebreaker. You have little to fear.”"}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“Oh, I ain’t afraid, gov’nor. All for the good of the cause. The streets
is going to run with blood, so they say.” He spoke with a grim relish.
“Dreams of it, sometimes, I does. And diamonds and pearls rolling about
in the gutter for anyone to pick up!”"}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "Tommy heard a chair shifted. Then Number One spoke:"}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "“Then all is arranged. We are assured of success?”"}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“I--think so.” But the German spoke with less than his usual confidence."}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "Number One’s voice held suddenly a dangerous quality:"}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "“What has gone wrong?”"}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“Nothing; but----”"}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": "“But what?”"}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": "“The Labour leaders. done to discredit the Government in their eyes, I’m not sure that they
haven’t got a sneaking faith and belief in it.”"}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": "“But----”"}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "“I know. They abuse it unceasingly. But, on the whole, public opinion

certain document in existence which assured success.”"}, {"paragraph": 91, "text": "“That is so. If that document were placed before the leaders, the result
would be immediate. They would publish it broadcast throughout England,
and declare for the revolution without a moment’s hesitation. The
Government would be broken finally and completely.”"}, {"paragraph": 92, "text": "“Then what more do you want?”"}, {"paragraph": 93, "text": "“The document itself,” said the German bluntly."}, {"paragraph": 94, "text": "“Ah! It is not in your possession? But you know where it is?”"}, {"paragraph": 95, "text": "“No.”"}, {"paragraph": 96, "text": "“Does anyone know where it is?”"}, {"paragraph": 97, "text": "“One person--perhaps. No money--no results!”"}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "Another voice which Tommy rather thought was that of Boris replied:"}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“Will you guarantee that there _are_ results?”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“In a month from now--sooner or later as you wish--I will guarantee you such a reign of terror in Ireland as shall shake the British Empire to its foundations.”"}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "Then came the soft, sibilant accents of Number One:"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“Good! You shall have the money. Boris, you will see to that.”"}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“I guess that’ll be all right!” said a new voice, with a transatlantic intonation, “though things are getting a mite difficult.”"}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "Tommy felt that Boris had shrugged his shoulders as he answered:"}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“Does that matter, since the money only nominally comes from the States?”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“The chief difficulty is the landing of the ammunition,” said the Sinn Feiner. “The money is conveyed in easily enough--thanks to our colleague here.”"}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "Another voice, which Tommy fancied was that of the tall, commanding-looking man whose face had seemed familiar to him, said:"}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“Think of the feelings of Belfast if they could hear you!”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“That is settled, then,” said the sibilant tones. “Now, in the matter of the loan to an English newspaper, you have arranged the details satisfactorily, Boris?”"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "“I think so.”"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "Then the German broke the silence:"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“I am directed by--Mr. Brown, to place the summaries of the reports from the different unions before you. That of the miners is most satisfactory. We must hold back the railways.”"}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "“And--the date, my friend?” said Number One."}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“The 29th.”"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "The Russian seemed to consider:"}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "“That is rather soon.”"}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“I know. But it was settled by the principal Labour leaders, and we cannot seem to interfere too much. They must believe it to be entirely their own show.”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "The Russian laughed softly."}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“Yes, yes,” he said. “They are honest men--and that is their value to us.” He paused, and then repeated, as though the phrase pleased him: “Every revolution has had its honest men. They are soon disposed of afterwards.”"}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "The German resumed:"}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“Clymes must go. He is too far-seeing. Number Fourteen will see to that.”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "There was a hoarse murmur."}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“That’s all right, gov’nor. Suppose I’m nabbed.”"}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "“You will have the best legal talent to defend you,” replied the German quietly. “But in any case you will wear gloves fitted with the finger-prints of a notorious housebreaker.”"}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“Oh, I ain’t afraid, gov’nor. The streets is going to run with blood, so they say.” He spoke with a grim relish."}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "Then Number One spoke:"}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "“Then all is arranged. We are assured of success?”"}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "“I--think so.” But the German spoke with less than his usual confidence."}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "Number One’s voice held suddenly a dangerous quality:"}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": "“What has gone wrong?”"}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": "“The Labour leaders,” said the German. “If they do not declare a general strike on the 29th---- As you’ve said, they’re honest. I’m not sure that they haven’t got a sneaking faith and belief in the Government. They will not go against it.”"}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "The Russian’s fingers drummed on the table."}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“To the point, my friend. I was given to understand that there was a certain document in existence which assured success.”"}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "“That is so. If that document were placed before the leaders, they would declare for the revolution without a moment’s hesitation.”"}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“Then what more do you want?”"}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "“The document itself,” said the German bluntly."}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "“Ah! It is not in your possession? But you know where it is?”"}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“No.”"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "“Does anyone know where it is?”"}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“One person--perhaps. And we are not sure of that even.”"}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“Who is this person?”"}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“A girl.”"}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "Tommy held his breath."}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "“A girl?” The Russian’s voice rose contemptuously. “And you have not made her speak? In Russia we have ways of making a girl talk.”"}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“This case is different,” said the German sullenly."}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "“How--different? Where is the girl now?”"}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "“She is----”"}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "But Tommy heard no more. A crashing blow descended on his head, and all was darkness."}], "012.source": [{"paragraph": 1, "text": "DRESSED appropriately, Tuppence duly sallied forth for her “afternoon
out.” Albert was in temporary abeyance, but Tuppence went herself to the
stationer’s to make quite sure that nothing had come for her. Satisfied
on this point, she made her way to the _Ritz_. On inquiry she learnt
that Tommy had not yet returned. It was the answer she had expected, but
it was another nail in the coffin of her hopes. She resolved to appeal
to Mr. Carter, telling him when and where Tommy had started on his
quest, and asking him to do something to trace him. The prospect of
his aid revived her mercurial spirits, and she next inquired for Julius
Hersheimmer. The reply she got was to the effect that he had returned
about half an hour ago, but had gone out immediately."}, {"paragraph": 2, "text": "Tuppence’s spirits revived still more. It would be something to see
Julius. Perhaps he could devise some plan for finding out what
had become of Tommy. She wrote her note to Mr. Carter in Julius’s
sitting-room, and was just addressing the envelope when the door burst
open."}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": "“What the hell----” began Julius, but checked himself abruptly. “I beg
your pardon, Miss Tuppence. Those fools down at the office would have it
that Beresford wasn’t here any longer--hadn’t been here since Wednesday.
Is that so?”"}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "Tuppence nodded."}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "“You don’t know where he is?” she asked faintly."}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "“I? How should I know? I haven’t had one darned word from him, though I
wired him yesterday morning.”"}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "“I expect your wire’s at the office unopened.”"}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "“But where is he?”"}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“I don’t know. I hoped you might.”"}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "“I tell you I haven’t had one darned word from him since we parted at
the depot on Wednesday.”"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "“What depot?”"}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "“Waterloo. Your London and South Western road.”"}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "“Waterloo?” frowned Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "“Why, yes. Didn’t he tell you?”"}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "“I haven’t seen him either,” replied Tuppence impatiently. “Go on about
Waterloo. What were you doing there?”"}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "“He gave me a call. Over the phone. Told me to get a move on, and
hustle. Said he was trailing two crooks.”"}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“Oh!” said Tuppence, her eyes opening. “I see. Go on.”"}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "“I hurried along right away. Beresford was there. He pointed out the
crooks. The big one was mine, the guy you bluffed. Tommy shoved a ticket
into my hand and told me to get aboard the cars. He was going to sleuth
the other crook.” Julius paused. “I thought for sure you’d know all
this.”"}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "“Julius,” said Tuppence firmly, “stop walking up and down. It makes me
giddy. Sit down in that armchair, and tell me the whole story with as
few fancy turns of speech as possible.”"}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "Mr. Hersheimmer obeyed."}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "“Sure,” he said. “Where shall I begin?”"}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "“Where you left off. At Waterloo.”"}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“Well,” began Julius, “I got into one of your dear old-fashioned
first-class British compartments. The train was just off. First thing I
knew a guard came along and informed me mighty politely that I wasn’t
in a smoking-carriage. I handed him out half a dollar, and that settled
that. I did a bit of prospecting along the corridor to the next coach.
Whittington was there right enough. When I saw the skunk, with his big
sleek fat face, and thought of poor little Jane in his clutches, I felt
real mad that I hadn’t got a gun with me. I’d have tickled him up some."}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "“We got to Bournemouth all right. Whittington took a cab and gave the
name of an hotel. I did likewise, and we drove up within three minutes
of each other. He hired a room, and I hired one too. So far it was all
plain sailing. He hadn’t the remotest notion that anyone was on to him.
Well, he just sat around in the hotel lounge, reading the papers and so
on, till it was time for dinner. He didn’t hurry any over that either."}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "“I began to think that there was nothing doing, that he’d just come on
the trip for his health, but I remembered that he hadn’t changed for
dinner, though it was by way of being a slap-up hotel, so it seemed
likely enough that he’d be going out on his real business afterwards."}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "“Sure enough, about nine o’clock, so he did. Took a car across the
town--mighty pretty place by the way, I guess I’ll take Jane there for
a spell when I find her--and then paid it off and struck out along those
pine-woods on the top of the cliff. I was there too, you understand.
We walked, maybe, for half an hour. There’s a lot of villas all the way
along, but by degrees they seemed to get more and more thinned out, and
in the end we got to one that seemed the last of the bunch. Big house it
was, with a lot of piny grounds around it."}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "“It was a pretty black night, and the carriage drive up to the house was
dark as pitch. I could hear him ahead, though I couldn’t see him. I
had to walk carefully in case he might get on to it that he was being
followed. I turned a curve and I was just in time to see him ring the
bell and get admitted to the house. I just stopped where I was. It was
beginning to rain, and I was soon pretty near soaked through. Also, it
was almighty cold."}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "“Whittington didn’t come out again, and by and by I got kind of restive,
and began to mouch around. All the ground floor windows were shuttered
tight, but upstairs, on the first floor (it was a two-storied house) I
noticed a window with a light burning and the curtains not drawn."}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "“Now, just opposite to that window, there was a tree growing. It was
about thirty foot away from the house, maybe, and I sort of got it into
my head that, if I climbed up that tree, I’d very likely be able to see
into that room. Of course, I knew there was no reason why Whittington
should be in that room rather than in any other--less reason, in fact,
for the betting would be on his being in one of the reception-rooms
downstairs. But I guess I’d got the hump from standing so long in the
rain, and anything seemed better than going on doing nothing. So I
started up."}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "“It wasn’t so easy, by a long chalk! The rain had made the boughs mighty
slippery, and it was all I could do to keep a foothold, but bit by bit I
managed it, until at last there I was level with the window."}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "“But then I was disappointed. I was too far to the left. I could only
see sideways into the room. A bit of curtain, and a yard of wallpaper
was all I could command. Well, that wasn’t any manner of good to me, but
just as I was going to give it up, and climb down ignominiously, some
one inside moved and threw his shadow on my little bit of wall--and, by
gum, it was Whittington!"}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“After that, my blood was up. I’d just _got_ to get a look into that
room. It was up to me to figure out how. I noticed that there was a long
branch running out from the tree in the right direction. If I could only
swarm about half-way along it, the proposition would be solved. But it
was mighty uncertain whether it would bear my weight. I decided I’d
just got to risk that, and I started. Very cautiously, inch by inch, I
crawled along. The bough creaked and swayed in a nasty fashion, and it
didn’t do to think of the drop below, but at last I got safely to where
I wanted to be."}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“The room was medium-sized, furnished in a kind of bare hygienic way.
There was a table with a lamp on it in the middle of the room, and
sitting at that table, facing towards me, was Whittington right enough.
He was talking to a woman dressed as a hospital nurse. She was sitting
with her back to me, so I couldn’t see her face. Although the blinds
were up, the window itself was shut, so I couldn’t catch a word of what
they said. Whittington seemed to be doing all the talking, and the nurse
just listened. Now and then she nodded, and sometimes she’d shake
her head, as though she were answering questions. He seemed very
emphatic--once or twice he beat with his fist on the table. The rain had
stopped now, and the sky was clearing in that sudden way it does."}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“Presently, he seemed to get to the end of what he was saying. He got
up, and so did she. He looked towards the window and asked something--I
guess it was whether it was raining. Anyway, she came right across and
looked out. Just then the moon came out from behind the clouds. I
was scared the woman would catch sight of me, for I was full in the
moonlight. I tried to move back a bit. The jerk I gave was too much for
that rotten old branch. With an almighty crash, down it came, and Julius
P. Hersheimmer with it!”"}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“Oh, Julius,” breathed Tuppence, “how exciting! Go on.”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“Well, luckily for me, I pitched down into a good soft bed of earth--but
it put me out of action for the time, sure enough. The next thing I
knew, I was lying in bed with a hospital nurse (not Whittington’s one)
on one side of me, and a little black-bearded man with gold glasses,
and medical man written all over him, on the other. He rubbed his hands
together, and raised his eyebrows as I stared at him. ‘Ah!’ he said. ‘So
our young friend is coming round again. Capital. Capital.’"}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“I did the usual stunt. Said: ‘What’s happened?’ And ‘Where am I?’ But
I knew the answer to the last well enough. There’s no moss growing on
my brain. ‘I think that’ll do for the present, sister,’ said the little
man, and the nurse left the room in a sort of brisk well-trained way.
But I caught her handing me out a look of deep curiosity as she passed
through the door."}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "“That look of hers gave me an idea. ‘Now then, doc,’ I said, and tried
to sit up in bed, but my right foot gave me a nasty twinge as I did so.
‘A slight sprain,’ explained the doctor. ‘Nothing serious. You’ll be
about again in a couple of days.’”"}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“I noticed you walked lame,” interpolated Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "Julius nodded, and continued:"}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "“‘How did it happen?’ I asked again. He replied dryly. ‘You fell, with
a considerable portion of one of my trees, into one of my newly planted
flower-beds.’"}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“I liked the man. He seemed to have a sense of humour. I felt sure that
he, at least, was plumb straight. ‘Sure, doc,’ I said, ‘I’m sorry about
the tree, and I guess the new bulbs will be on me. But perhaps you’d
like to know what I was doing in your garden?’ ‘I think the facts do
call for an explanation,’ he replied. ‘Well, to begin with, I wasn’t
after the spoons.’"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“He smiled. ‘My first theory. But I soon altered my mind. By the way,
you are an American, are you not?’ I told him my name. ‘And you?’ ‘I am
Dr. Hall, and this, as you doubtless know, is my private nursing home.’"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "“I didn’t know, but I wasn’t going to put him wise. I was just thankful
for the information. I liked the man, and I felt he was straight, but
I wasn’t going to give him the whole story. For one thing he probably
wouldn’t have believed it."}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“I made up my mind in a flash. ‘Why, doctor,’ I said, ‘I guess I feel
an almighty fool, but I owe it to you to let you know that it wasn’t
the Bill Sikes business I was up to.’ Then I went on and mumbled out
something about a girl. I trotted out the stern guardian business, and a
nervous breakdown, and finally explained that I had fancied I recognized
her among the patients at the home, hence my nocturnal adventures. I
guess it was just the kind of story he was expecting. ‘Quite a romance,’
he said genially, when I’d finished. ‘Now, doc,’ I went on, ‘will you
be frank with me? Have you here now, or have you had here at any time,
a young girl called Jane Finn?’ He repeated the name thoughtfully. ‘Jane
Finn?’ he said. ‘No.’"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“I was chagrined, and I guess I showed it. ‘You are sure?’ ‘Quite sure,
Mr. Hersheimmer. It is an uncommon name, and I should not have been
likely to forget it.’"}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "“Well, that was flat. It laid me out for a space. I’d kind of hoped
my search was at an end. ‘That’s that,’ I said at last. ‘Now, there’s
another matter. When I was hugging that darned branch I thought I
recognized an old friend of mine talking to one of your nurses.’ I
purposely didn’t mention any name because, of course, Whittington might
be calling himself something quite different down here, but the doctor
answered at once. ‘Mr. Whittington, perhaps?’ ‘That’s the fellow,’ I
replied. ‘What’s he doing down here? Don’t tell me _his_ nerves are out
of order?’"}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“Dr. Hall laughed. ‘No. He came down to see one of my nurses, Nurse
Edith, who is a niece of his.’ ‘Why, fancy that!’ I exclaimed. ‘Is he
still here?’ ‘No, he went back to town almost immediately.’ ‘What a
pity!’ I ejaculated. ‘But perhaps I could speak to his niece--Nurse
Edith, did you say her name was?’"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "“But the doctor shook his head. ‘I’m afraid that, too, is impossible.
Nurse Edith left with a patient to-night also.’ ‘I seem to be real
unlucky,’ I remarked. ‘Have you Mr. Whittington’s address in town?
I guess I’d like to look him up when I get back.’ ‘I don’t know his
address. I can write to Nurse Edith for it if you like.’ I thanked him.
‘Don’t say who it is wants it. I’d like to give him a little surprise.’"}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "“That was about all I could do for the moment. Of course, if the girl
was really Whittington’s niece, she might be too cute to fall into the
trap, but it was worth trying. Next thing I did was to write out a wire
to Beresford saying where I was, and that I was laid up with a sprained
foot, and telling him to come down if he wasn’t busy. I had to be
guarded in what I said. However, I didn’t hear from him, and my foot
soon got all right. It was only ricked, not really sprained, so to-day I
said good-bye to the little doctor chap, asked him to send me word if
he heard from Nurse Edith, and came right away back to town. Say, Miss
Tuppence, you’re looking mighty pale!”"}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“It’s Tommy,” said Tuppence. “What can have happened to him?”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "“Buck up, I guess he’s all right really. Why shouldn’t he be? See here,
it was a foreign-looking guy he went off after. Maybe they’ve gone
abroad--to Poland, or something like that?”"}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "Tuppence shook her head."}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "“He couldn’t without passports and things. Besides I’ve seen that man,
Boris Something, since. He dined with Mrs. Vandemeyer last night.”"}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“Mrs. Who?”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "“I forgot. Of course you don’t know all that.”"}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“I’m listening,” said Julius, and gave vent to his favourite expression.
“Put me wise.”"}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "Tuppence thereupon related the events of the last two days. Julius’s
astonishment and admiration were unbounded."}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“Bully for you! Fancy you a menial. It just tickles me to death!” Then
he added seriously: “But say now, I don’t like it, Miss Tuppence, I sure
don’t. You’re just as plucky as they make ‘em, but I wish you’d keep
right out of this. These crooks we’re up against would as soon croak a
girl as a man any day.”"}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "“Do you think I’m afraid?” said Tuppence indignantly, valiantly
repressing memories of the steely glitter in Mrs. Vandemeyer’s eyes."}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "“I said before you were darned plucky. But that doesn’t alter facts.”"}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "“Oh, bother _me!_” said Tuppence impatiently. “Let’s think about what
can have happened to Tommy. I’ve written to Mr. Carter about it,” she
added, and told him the gist of her letter."}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "Julius nodded gravely."}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": "“I guess that’s good as far as it goes. But it’s for us to get busy and
do something.”"}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": "“What can we do?” asked Tuppence, her spirits rising."}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "“I guess we’d better get on the track of Boris. You say he’s been to
your place. Is he likely to come again?”"}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“He might. I really don’t know.”"}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "“I see. Well, I guess I’d better buy a car, a slap-up one, dress as a
chauffeur and hang about outside. Then if Boris comes, you could make
some kind of signal, and I’d trail him. How’s that?”"}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“Splendid, but he mightn’t come for weeks.”"}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "“We’ll have to chance that. I’m glad you like the plan.” He rose."}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "“Where are you going?”"}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“To buy the car, of course,” replied Julius, surprised. “What make do
you like? I guess you’ll do some riding in it before we’ve finished.”"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "“Oh,” said Tuppence faintly, “I _like_ Rolls-Royces, but----”"}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“Sure,” agreed Julius. “What you say goes. I’ll get one.”"}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“But you can’t at once,” cried Tuppence. “People wait ages sometimes.”"}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“Little Julius doesn’t,” affirmed Mr. Hersheimmer. “Don’t you worry any.
I’ll be round in the car in half an hour.”"}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "Tuppence got up."}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "“You’re awfully good, Julius. But I can’t help feeling that it’s rather
a forlorn hope. I’m really pinning my faith to Mr. Carter.”"}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“Then I shouldn’t.”"}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "“Why?”"}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "“Just an idea of mine.”"}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“Oh; but he must do something. There’s no one else. By the way, I forgot
to tell you of a queer thing that happened this morning.”"}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": "And she narrated her encounter with Sir James Peel Edgerton. Julius was
interested."}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": "“What did the guy mean, do you think?” he asked."}, {"paragraph": 85, "text": "“I don’t quite know,” said Tuppence meditatively. “But I think that, in
an ambiguous, legal, without prejudishish lawyer’s way, he was trying to
warn me.”"}, {"paragraph": 86, "text": "“Why should he?”"}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": "“I don’t know,” confessed Tuppence. “But he looked kind, and
simply awfully clever. I wouldn’t mind going to him and telling him
everything.”"}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "Somewhat to her surprise, Julius negatived the idea sharply."}, {"paragraph": 89, "text": "“See here,” he said, “we don’t want any lawyers mixed up in this. That
guy couldn’t help us any.”"}, {"paragraph": 90, "text": "“Well, I believe he could,” reiterated Tuppence obstinately."}, {"paragraph": 91, "text": "“Don’t you think it. So long. I’ll be back in half an hour.”"}, {"paragraph": 92, "text": "Thirty-five minutes had elapsed when Julius returned. He took Tuppence
by the arm, and walked her to the window."}, {"paragraph": 93, "text": "“There she is.”"}, {"paragraph": 94, "text": "“Oh!” said Tuppence with a note of reverence in her voice, as she gazed
down at the enormous car."}, {"paragraph": 95, "text": "“She’s some pace-maker, I can tell you,” said Julius complacently."}, {"paragraph": 96, "text": "“How did you get it?” gasped Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 97, "text": "“She was just being sent home to some bigwig.”"}, {"paragraph": 98, "text": "“Well?”"}, {"paragraph": 99, "text": "“I went round to his house,” said Julius. “I said that I reckoned a car
like that was worth every penny of twenty thousand dollars. Then I told
him that it was worth just about fifty thousand dollars to me if he’d
get out.”"}, {"paragraph": 100, "text": "“Well?” said Tuppence, intoxicated."}, {"paragraph": 101, "text": "“Well,” returned Julius, “he got out, that’s all.”"}], "012.revision": [{"paragraph": 1, "text": "DRESSED appropriately, Tuppence duly sallied forth for her “afternoon out.” Albert was in temporary abeyance, but Tuppence went herself to the stationer’s to make quite sure that nothing had come for her. The big one was mine, the guy you bluffed. Tommy shoved a ticket into my hand and told me to get aboard the cars. He was going to sleuth the other crook.”"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "“Julius,” said Tuppence firmly, “stop walking up and down. It makes me giddy. Sit down in that armchair, and tell me the whole story with as few fancy turns of speech as possible.”"}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "“Well,” began Julius, “I got into one of your dear old-fashioned first-class British compartments. I did a bit of prospecting along the corridor to the next coach. Whittington was there right enough."}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "“We got to Bournemouth all right. Whittington took a cab and gave the name of an hotel. I did likewise. About nine o’clock he went out. Took a car across the town, and then paid it off and struck out along those pine-woods on the top of the cliff. There’s a lot of villas all the way along, and in the end we got to one that seemed the last of the bunch."}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "“I turned a curve and I was just in time to see him ring the bell and get admitted to the house. It was beginning to rain, and I was soon pretty near soaked through."}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "“Whittington didn’t come out again, and by and by I got kind of restive. All the ground floor windows were shuttered tight, but upstairs I noticed a window with a light burning and the curtains not drawn. Just opposite that window there was a tree growing. So I started up."}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "“Bit by bit I managed it, until at last I was level with the window. But I was too far to the left. A bit of curtain, and a yard of wallpaper was all I could command. Just as I was going to give it up, some one inside moved and threw his shadow on my little bit of wall--and, by gum, it was Whittington!"}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“After that, my blood was up. There was a long branch running out in the right direction, but it was mighty uncertain whether it would bear my weight. Very cautiously, inch by inch, I crawled along, and at last I got to where I wanted to be."}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "“Sitting at a table, facing towards me, was Whittington right enough. He was talking to a woman dressed as a hospital nurse. She was sitting with her back to me, so I couldn’t see her face. The window was shut, so I couldn’t catch a word of what they said. He seemed very emphatic--once or twice he beat with his fist on the table."}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "“Presently he got up, and so did she. She came right across and looked out. Just then the moon came out from behind the clouds. I was scared the woman would catch sight of me, for I was full in the moonlight. I tried to move back a bit. The jerk I gave was too much for that rotten old branch. With an almighty crash, down it came, and Julius P. Hersheimmer with it!”"}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "“Well, luckily for me, I pitched down into a good soft bed of earth--but it put me out of action for the time. The next thing I knew, I was lying in bed with a hospital nurse (not Whittington’s one) on one side of me, and a little black-bearded man with gold glasses, and medical man written all over him, on the other. I tried to sit up, but my right foot gave me a nasty twinge. ‘A slight sprain,’ explained the doctor. ‘Nothing serious.’”"}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "“I noticed you walked lame,” interpolated Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "Julius nodded, and continued:"}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“‘How did it happen?’ I asked. He replied dryly. ‘You fell, with a considerable portion of one of my trees, into one of my newly planted flower-beds.’"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "“I liked the man. He seemed to have a sense of humour. I felt sure that he, at least, was plumb straight. ‘You are an American, are you not?’ he asked. I told him my name. ‘And you?’ ‘I am Dr. Hall, and this, as you doubtless know, is my private nursing home.’"}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "“I didn’t know, but I wasn’t going to put him wise. So I mumbled out something about a girl. I trotted out the stern guardian business, and a nervous breakdown, and explained that I had fancied I recognized her among the patients at the home. ‘Quite a romance,’ he said genially. ‘Now, doc,’ I went on, ‘will you be frank with me? Have you here now, or have you had here at any time, a young girl called Jane Finn?’ He repeated the name thoughtfully. ‘Jane Finn?’ he said. ‘No.’"}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "“I was chagrined, and I guess I showed it. ‘You are sure?’ ‘Quite sure, Mr. Hersheimmer. It is an uncommon name, and I should not have been likely to forget it.’"}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "“Well, that was flat. ‘Now, there’s another matter,’ I said. ‘When I was hugging that darned branch I thought I recognized an old friend of mine talking to one of your nurses.’ I purposely didn’t mention any name, but the doctor answered at once. ‘Mr. Whittington, perhaps?’ ‘That’s the fellow. Don’t tell me _his_ nerves are out of order?’"}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "“Dr. Hall laughed. ‘No. He came down to see one of my nurses, Nurse Edith, who is a niece of his.’ ‘Is he still here?’ ‘No, he went back to town almost immediately.’ ‘But perhaps I could speak to his niece?’"}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "“But the doctor shook his head. ‘I’m afraid that, too, is impossible. Nurse Edith left with a patient to-night also.’ ‘Have you Mr. Whittington’s address in town?’ ‘I don’t know his address. I can write to Nurse Edith for it if you like.’ I thanked him. ‘Don’t say who it is wants it. I’d like to give him a little surprise.’"}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "“Next thing I wrote out a wire to Beresford saying where I was, and telling him to come down if he wasn’t busy. However, I didn’t hear from him, so to-day I said good-bye to the little doctor chap, asked him to send me word if he heard from Nurse Edith, and came right away back to town. Say, Miss Tuppence, you’re looking mighty pale!”"}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "“It’s Tommy,” said Tuppence. “What can have happened to him?”"}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“Buck up, I guess he’s all right really. See here, it was a foreign-looking guy he went off after.”"}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“I’ve seen that man, Boris Something, since. He dined with Mrs. Vandemeyer last night.”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“Mrs. Who?” asked Julius."}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“I forgot. Of course you don’t know all that.”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“I’m listening,” said Julius. “Put me wise.”"}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "Tuppence thereupon related the events of the last two days. Julius’s astonishment and admiration were unbounded."}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "“Bully for you! Fancy you a menial. It just tickles me to death!” Then he added seriously: “But say now, I don’t like it, Miss Tuppence. These crooks we’re up against would as soon croak a girl as a man any day.”"}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“Do you think I’m afraid?” said Tuppence indignantly, valiantly repressing memories of the steely glitter in Mrs. Vandemeyer’s eyes. “Let’s think about what can have happened to Tommy. I’ve written to Mr. Carter about it.”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“I guess that’s good as far as it goes. But I guess we’d better get on the track of Boris. Is he likely to come again?”"}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "“He might. I really don’t know,” said Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“Well, I guess I’d better buy a car, a slap-up one, dress as a chauffeur and hang about outside. Then if Boris comes, you could make some kind of signal, and I’d trail him. What make do you like?”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“Oh,” said Tuppence faintly, “I _like_ Rolls-Royces, but----”"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "“Sure,” agreed Julius. “I’ll be round in the car in half an hour.”"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“You’re awfully good, Julius. But I’m really pinning my faith to Mr. Carter.”"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“Then I shouldn’t,” said Julius."}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "“Why?”"}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“Just an idea of mine.”"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "“Oh; but he must do something. There’s no one else,” said Tuppence. And she narrated her encounter that morning with Sir James Peel Edgerton."}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "“What did the guy mean, do you think?” Julius asked."}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“I don’t quite know,” said Tuppence meditatively. “But I think that, in an ambiguous, legal, without prejudishish lawyer’s way, he was trying to warn me. He looked kind, and simply awfully clever. I wouldn’t mind going to him and telling him everything.”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "Somewhat to her surprise, Julius negatived the idea sharply."}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“See here,” he said, “we don’t want any lawyers mixed up in this. That guy couldn’t help us any.”"}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "“Well, I believe he could,” reiterated Tuppence obstinately."}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“Don’t you think it. So long. I’ll be back in half an hour.”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "Thirty-five minutes had elapsed when Julius returned. He took Tuppence by the arm, and walked her to the window."}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“There she is.”"}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "“Oh!” said Tuppence with a note of reverence in her voice, as she gazed down at the enormous car. “How did you get it?”"}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“She was just being sent home to some bigwig,” said Julius. “I went round to his house. I said that I reckoned a car like that was worth every penny of twenty thousand dollars. Then I told him that it was worth just about fifty thousand dollars to me if he’d get out.”"}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "“Well?” said Tuppence, intoxicated."}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "“Well,” returned Julius, “he got out, that’s all.”"}], "025.source": [{"paragraph": 1, "text": "IN his suite at Claridge’s, Kramenin reclined on a couch and dictated to
his secretary in sibilant Russian."}, {"paragraph": 2, "text": "Presently the telephone at the secretary’s elbow purred, and he took up
the receiver, spoke for a minute or two, then turned to his employer."}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": "“Some one below is asking for you.”"}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "“Who is it?”"}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "“He gives the name of Mr. Julius P. Hersheimmer.”"}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "“Hersheimmer,” repeated Kramenin thoughtfully. “I have heard that name
before.”"}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "“His father was one of the steel kings of America,” explained the
secretary, whose business it was to know everything. “This young man
must be a millionaire several times over.”"}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "The other’s eyes narrowed appreciatively."}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“You had better go down and see him, Ivan. Find out what he wants.”"}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "The secretary obeyed, closing the door noiselessly behind him. In a few
minutes he returned."}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "“He declines to state his business--says it is entirely private and
personal, and that he must see you.”"}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "“A millionaire several times over,” murmured Kramenin. “Bring him up, my
dear Ivan.”"}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "The secretary left the room once more, and returned escorting Julius."}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "“Monsieur Kramenin?” said the latter abruptly."}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "The Russian, studying him attentively with his pale venomous eyes,
bowed."}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "“Pleased to meet you,” said the American. “I’ve got some very important
business I’d like to talk over with you, if I can see you alone.” He
looked pointedly at the other."}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“My secretary, Monsieur Grieber, from whom I have no secrets.”"}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "“That may be so--but I have,” said Julius dryly. “So I’d be obliged if
you’d tell him to scoot.”"}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "“Ivan,” said the Russian softly, “perhaps you would not mind retiring
into the next room----”"}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "“The next room won’t do,” interrupted Julius. “I know these ducal
suites--and I want this one plumb empty except for you and me. Send him
round to a store to buy a penn’orth of peanuts.”"}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "Though not particularly enjoying the American’s free and easy manner
of speech, Kramenin was devoured by curiosity. “Will your business take
long to state?”"}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "“Might be an all night job if you caught on.”"}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“Very good, Ivan. I shall not require you again this evening. Go to the
theatre--take a night off.”"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "“Thank you, your excellency.”"}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "The secretary bowed and departed."}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "Julius stood at the door watching his retreat. Finally, with a satisfied
sigh, he closed it, and came back to his position in the centre of the
room."}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "“Now, Mr. Hersheimmer, perhaps you will be so kind as to come to the
point?”"}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "“I guess that won’t take a minute,” drawled Julius. Then, with an abrupt
change of manner: “Hands up--or I shoot!”"}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "For a moment Kramenin stared blindly into the big automatic, then, with
almost comical haste, he flung up his hands above his head. In that
instant Julius had taken his measure. The man he had to deal with was an
abject physical coward--the rest would be easy."}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "“This is an outrage,” cried the Russian in a high hysterical voice. “An
outrage! Do you mean to kill me?”"}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "“Not if you keep your voice down. Don’t go edging sideways towards that
bell. That’s better.”"}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“What do you want? Do nothing rashly. Remember my life is of the utmost
value to my country. I may have been maligned----”"}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“I reckon,” said Julius, “that the man who let daylight into you would
be doing humanity a good turn. But you needn’t worry any. I’m not
proposing to kill you this trip--that is, if you’re reasonable.”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "The Russian quailed before the stern menace in the other’s eyes. He
passed his tongue over his dry lips."}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“What do you want? Money?”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“No. I want Jane Finn.”"}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“Jane Finn? I--never heard of her!”"}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "“You’re a darned liar! You know perfectly who I mean.”"}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“I tell you I’ve never heard of the girl.”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“And I tell you,” retorted Julius, “that Little Willie here is just
hopping mad to go off!”"}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "The Russian wilted visibly."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“You wouldn’t dare----”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“Oh, yes, I would, son!”"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "Kramenin must have recognized something in the voice that carried
conviction, for he said sullenly:"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“Well? Granted I do know who you mean--what of it?”"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“You will tell me now--right here--where she is to be found.”"}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "Kramenin shook his head."}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“I daren’t.”"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "“Why not?”"}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "“I daren’t. You ask an impossibility.”"}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“Afraid, eh? Of whom? Mr. Brown? Ah, that tickles you up! There is such
a person, then? I doubted it. And the mere mention of him scares you
stiff!”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "“I have seen him,” said the Russian slowly. “Spoken to him face to face.
I did not know it until afterwards. He was one of a crowd. I should not
know him again. Who is he really? I do not know. But I know this--he is
a man to fear.”"}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“He’ll never know,” said Julius."}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "“He knows everything--and his vengeance is swift. Even
I--Kramenin!--would not be exempt!”"}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“Then you won’t do as I ask you?”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "“You ask an impossibility.”"}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“Sure that’s a pity for you,” said Julius cheerfully. “But the world in
general will benefit.” He raised the revolver."}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "“Stop,” shrieked the Russian. “You cannot mean to shoot me?”"}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“Of course I do. I’ve always heard you Revolutionists held life cheap,
but it seems there’s a difference when it’s your own life in question.
I gave you just one chance of saving your dirty skin, and that you
wouldn’t take!”"}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "“They would kill me!”"}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "“Well,” said Julius pleasantly, “it’s up to you. But I’ll just say this.
Little Willie here is a dead cert, and if I was you I’d take a sporting
chance with Mr. Brown!”"}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "“You will hang if you shoot me,” muttered the Russian irresolutely."}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "“No, stranger, that’s where you’re wrong. You forget the dollars. A
big crowd of solicitors will get busy, and they’ll get some high-brow
doctors on the job, and the end of it all will be that they’ll say my
brain was unhinged. I shall spend a few months in a quiet sanatorium, my
mental health will improve, the doctors will declare me sane again, and
all will end happily for little Julius. I guess I can bear a few months’
retirement in order to rid the world of you, but don’t you kid yourself
I’ll hang for it!”"}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": "The Russian believed him. Corrupt himself, he believed implicitly in the
power of money. He had read of American murder trials running much on
the lines indicated by Julius. He had bought and sold justice himself.
This virile young American, with the significant drawling voice, had the
whip hand of him."}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": "“I’m going to count five,” continued Julius, “and I guess, if you let me
get past four, you needn’t worry any about Mr. Brown. Maybe he’ll send
some flowers to the funeral, but _you_ won’t smell them! Are you ready?
I’ll begin. One--two--three--four----”"}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "The Russian interrupted with a shriek:"}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“Do not shoot. I will do all you wish.”"}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "Julius lowered the revolver."}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“I thought you’d hear sense. Where is the girl?”"}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "“At Gatehouse, in Kent. Astley Priors, the place is called.”"}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "“Is she a prisoner there?”"}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“She’s not allowed to leave the house--though it’s safe enough really.
The little fool has lost her memory, curse her!”"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "“That’s been annoying for you and your friends, I reckon. What about the
other girl, the one you decoyed away over a week ago?”"}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“She’s there too,” said the Russian sullenly."}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“That’s good,” said Julius. “Isn’t it all panning out beautifully? And a
lovely night for the run!”"}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“What run?” demanded Kramenin, with a stare."}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "“Down to Gatehouse, sure. I hope you’re fond of motoring?”"}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "“What do you mean? I refuse to go.”"}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“Now don’t get mad. You must see I’m not such a kid as to leave you
here. You’d ring up your friends on that telephone first thing! Ah!” He
observed the fall on the other’s face. “You see, you’d got it all fixed.
No, sir, you’re coming along with me. This your bedroom next door here?
Walk right in. Little Willie and I will come behind. Put on a thick
coat, that’s right. Fur lined? And you a Socialist! Now we’re ready. We
walk downstairs and out through the hall to where my car’s waiting. And
don’t you forget I’ve got you covered every inch of the way. I can shoot
just as well through my coat pocket. One word, or a glance even, at one
of those liveried menials, and there’ll sure be a strange face in the
Sulphur and Brimstone Works!”"}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "Together they descended the stairs, and passed out to the waiting car.
The Russian was shaking with rage. The hotel servants surrounded them.
A cry hovered on his lips, but at the last minute his nerve failed him.
The American was a man of his word."}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "When they reached the car, Julius breathed a sigh of relief. The
danger-zone was passed. Fear had successfully hypnotized the man by his
side."}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“Get in,” he ordered. Then as he caught the other’s sidelong glance,
“No, the chauffeur won’t help you any. Naval man. Was on a submarine in
Russia when the Revolution broke out. A brother of his was murdered by
your people. George!”"}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": "“Yes, sir?” The chauffeur turned his head."}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": "“This gentleman is a Russian Bolshevik. We don’t want to shoot him, but
it may be necessary. You understand?”"}, {"paragraph": 85, "text": "“Perfectly, sir.”"}, {"paragraph": 86, "text": "“I want to go to Gatehouse in Kent. Know the road at all?”"}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": "“Yes, sir, it will be about an hour and a half’s run.”"}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "“Make it an hour. I’m in a hurry.”"}, {"paragraph": 89, "text": "“I’ll do my best, sir.” The car shot forward through the traffic."}, {"paragraph": 90, "text": "Julius ensconced himself comfortably by the side of his victim. He kept
his hand in the pocket of his coat, but his manner was urbane to the
last degree."}, {"paragraph": 91, "text": "“There was a man I shot once in Arizona----” he began cheerfully."}, {"paragraph": 92, "text": "At the end of the hour’s run the unfortunate Kramenin was more dead than
alive. In succession to the anecdote of the Arizona man, there had been
a tough from ‘Frisco, and an episode in the Rockies. Julius’s narrative
style, if not strictly accurate, was picturesque!"}, {"paragraph": 93, "text": "Slowing down, the chauffeur called over his shoulder that they were just
coming into Gatehouse. Julius bade the Russian direct them. His plan was
to drive straight up to the house. There Kramenin was to ask for the two
girls. Julius explained to him that Little Willie would not be tolerant
of failure. Kramenin, by this time, was as putty in the other’s hands.
The terrific pace they had come had still further unmanned him. He had
given himself up for dead at every corner."}, {"paragraph": 94, "text": "The car swept up the drive, and stopped before the porch. The chauffeur
looked round for orders."}, {"paragraph": 95, "text": "“Turn the car first, George. Then ring the bell, and get back to your
place. Keep the engine going, and be ready to scoot like hell when I
give the word.”"}, {"paragraph": 96, "text": "“Very good, sir.”"}, {"paragraph": 97, "text": "The front door was opened by the butler. Kramenin felt the muzzle of the
revolver pressed against his ribs."}, {"paragraph": 98, "text": "“Now,” hissed Julius. “And be careful.”"}, {"paragraph": 99, "text": "The Russian beckoned. His lips were white, and his voice was not very
steady:"}, {"paragraph": 100, "text": "“It is I--Kramenin! Bring down the girl at once! There is no time to
lose!”"}, {"paragraph": 101, "text": "Whittington had come down the steps. He uttered an exclamation of
astonishment at seeing the other."}, {"paragraph": 102, "text": "“You! What’s up? Surely you know the plan----”"}, {"paragraph": 103, "text": "Kramenin interrupted him, using the words that have created many
unnecessary panics:"}, {"paragraph": 104, "text": "“We have been betrayed! Plans must be abandoned. We must save our own
skins. The girl! And at once! It’s our only chance.”"}, {"paragraph": 105, "text": "Whittington hesitated, but for hardly a moment."}, {"paragraph": 106, "text": "“You have orders--from _him?_”"}, {"paragraph": 107, "text": "“Naturally! Should I be here otherwise? Hurry! There is no time to be
lost. The other little fool had better come too.”"}, {"paragraph": 108, "text": "Whittington turned and ran back into the house. The agonizing minutes
went by. Then--two figures hastily huddled in cloaks appeared on the
steps and were hustled into the car. The smaller of the two was inclined
to resist and Whittington shoved her in unceremoniously. Julius leaned
forward, and in doing so the light from the open door lit up his face.
Another man on the steps behind Whittington gave a startled exclamation.
Concealment was at an end."}, {"paragraph": 109, "text": "“Get a move on, George,” shouted Julius."}, {"paragraph": 110, "text": "The chauffeur slipped in his clutch, and with a bound the car started."}, {"paragraph": 111, "text": "The man on the steps uttered an oath. His hand went to his pocket. There
was a flash and a report. The bullet just missed the taller girl by an
inch."}, {"paragraph": 112, "text": "“Get down, Jane,” cried Julius. “Flat on the bottom of the car.” He
thrust her sharply forward, then standing up, he took careful aim and
fired."}, {"paragraph": 113, "text": "“Have you hit him?” cried Tuppence eagerly."}, {"paragraph": 114, "text": "“Sure,” replied Julius. “He isn’t killed, though. Skunks like that take
a lot of killing. Are you all right, Tuppence?”"}, {"paragraph": 115, "text": "“Of course I am. Where’s Tommy? And who’s this?” She indicated the
shivering Kramenin."}, {"paragraph": 116, "text": "“Tommy’s making tracks for the Argentine. I guess he thought you’d
turned up your toes. Steady through the gate, George! That’s right.
It’ll take ‘em at least five minutes to get busy after us. They’ll use
the telephone, I guess, so look out for snares ahead--and don’t take the
direct route. Who’s this, did you say, Tuppence? Let me present Monsieur
Kramenin. I persuaded him to come on the trip for his health.”"}, {"paragraph": 117, "text": "The Russian remained mute, still livid with terror."}, {"paragraph": 118, "text": "“But what made them let us go?” demanded Tuppence suspiciously."}, {"paragraph": 119, "text": "“I reckon Monsieur Kramenin here asked them so prettily they just
couldn’t refuse!”"}, {"paragraph": 120, "text": "This was too much for the Russian. He burst out vehemently:"}, {"paragraph": 121, "text": "“Curse you--curse you! They know now that I betrayed them. My life won’t
be safe for an hour in this country.”"}, {"paragraph": 122, "text": "“That’s so,” assented Julius. “I’d advise you to make tracks for Russia
right away.”"}, {"paragraph": 123, "text": "“Let me go, then,” cried the other. “I have done what you asked. Why do
you still keep me with you?”"}, {"paragraph": 124, "text": "“Not for the pleasure of your company. I guess you can get right off now
if you want to. I thought you’d rather I tooled you back to London.”"}, {"paragraph": 125, "text": "“You may never reach London,” snarled the other. “Let me go here and
now.”"}, {"paragraph": 126, "text": "“Sure thing. Pull up, George. The gentleman’s not making the return
trip. If I ever come to Russia, Monsieur Kramenin, I shall expect a
rousing welcome, and----”"}, {"paragraph": 127, "text": "But before Julius had finished his speech, and before the car had
finally halted, the Russian had swung himself out and disappeared into
the night."}, {"paragraph": 128, "text": "“Just a mite impatient to leave us,” commented Julius, as the car
gathered way again. “And no idea of saying good-bye politely to the
ladies. Say, Jane, you can get up on the seat now.”"}, {"paragraph": 129, "text": "For the first time the girl spoke."}, {"paragraph": 130, "text": "“How did you ‘persuade’ him?” she asked."}, {"paragraph": 131, "text": "Julius tapped his revolver."}, {"paragraph": 132, "text": "“Little Willie here takes the credit!”"}, {"paragraph": 133, "text": "“Splendid!” cried the girl. The colour surged into her face, her eyes
looked admiringly at Julius."}, {"paragraph": 134, "text": "“Annette and I didn’t know what was going to happen to us,” said
Tuppence. “Old Whittington hurried us off. _We_ thought it was lambs to
